A side-channel attack on machine learning models has received less attention compared to other types of attacks, yet it remains a significant concern. In this research, we present a novel method for inferring the inner workings of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) using power trace measurements obtained from low-level hardware components, such as multiplication and activation units. We successfully applied this method to the widely used LeNet network, a basic model utilized in digital image recognition, and a more complex ConvNet model optimized for the same task. The proposed attack demonstrates superior performance compared to other side-channel methods on these datasets.

To shorten polarization kernels through iterative partial distance removal,
establishing both loose and tight limits on the remaining sections of the curve
is necessary. Calculating these limits can be a challenging process, especially
in the cone of real positive semidefinite matrices, where a polarization kernel
is located. In this research, new methods for determining these bounds will be
described, along with explicit calculations for certain specific kernels.
Furthermore, a strategy for developing a systematic approach to shorten the
kernels of specific classes is outlined.

A new method for removing noise from 3D reflection seismic data has been developed, which involves self-supervised training of a denoising convolutional neural network using real-world data. However, early model training was found to be challenging due to noisy signal dominance, necessitating the use of a synthetic data training phase to improve performance on real-world data. By incorporating synthetic data training, the denoising model's ability to generalize on real-world data has been significantly enhanced, resulting in more accurate and efficient denoising capabilities. In comparison to existing approaches, the new method yields greater denoising efficacy without incurring additional computational costs. Its efficiency has been demonstrated by its ability to process a 48-squared square survey in under 30 minutes using a single NVIDIA 1080 Ti graphics card, even at the expense of greater computational resources.

In this study, we investigate the real photon emission process in lepton-proton scattering within the context of low-energy electron scattering. The contribution of real photon emission to the observed asymmetry in lepton-proton scattering is found to be the primary origin. The interaction cross-sections for lepton-proton scattering are also examined, with a note that we've limited our analysis to the lowest-order QED interactions. The aim of this research is to explore the potential of real photon emission for uncovering new physics limitations in the Standard Model through low-energy scattering experiments involving a single emitted photon.

The Mott insulators with spin-Pol'yanin ladders can exhibit unique correlations in their electronic structures, which are influenced by the spin-Pol'yanin spectrum. Our research demonstrates that both the doped and undoped Mott ladders display an anisotropic metal-insulator transition under varying conditions. The presence of spin-Pol'yanin ladders in the electronic structure significantly affects the low-energy states, making them more susceptible to charge fluctuations. The resulting low-energy charge excitations have a large spectral weight, which is responsible for the observed anisotropic transition. Notably, this anisotropic transition is consistent in both the doped and undoped Mott ladders, with their insulating states displaying gapped spectra. The study also shows that the strength of spin-Pol'yanin interactions influences the properties of the resulting phases. The research findings are consistent with the experimental results on La$_{1.65}$Sr$_{0.35}$CuS$_{0.82}$Ga$_{0.18}$Mo (La-PSG) material, which can be represented by a spin-Pol'yanin ladder model.

This study develops a method for estimating treatment effects using a continuous variable, ensuring robustness in a wide range of specific models, particularly those with nonlinear treatment impacts. Notably, our estimator achieves robustness without relying on specific assumptions about these models. Building upon a new model of nonlinear treatment effects, our findings also establish the validity of our approach in both controlled and uncontrolled conditions. In contrast to previous studies, our research addresses nonlinear effects and provides new insights into the reliability of instrumental variable estimates under different conditions.

Recent breakthroughs in starshade research have garnered significant recent attention. This paper highlights the benefits of integrating these advances into the astronomical community, including the creation of mutually beneficial tools and the application of novel techniques in observing starshades. The potential for cross-fertilization of concepts between starshades and other technologies, such as star simulators, is also explored.

The existence of suicidal texts online necessitates the development of a robust, high-quality training dataset to aid in identifying suicidal threats. A recent study created the Robin dataset, which consists of 7,985 annotated texts labeled by experts as either non-suicidal or containing a suicidal sentiment. This dataset features an improved annotation scheme compared to its predecessors, as it enables the expression of complex suicidal thoughts. As a result, the Robin dataset offers a vast collection of annotated examples, serving as the largest available collection for suicidal intent detection. An evaluation of 16 baseline models on this dataset revealed their potential to excel in this task. Furthermore, the authors propose a new approach, called knowledge distillation with fake data, which significantly enhances model performance. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the SentiNet dataset and demonstrates its efficacy on the Robin dataset.

A supersymmetric extension of the Schrödinger group acting on the superdomain leads to a constrained Wronskian system of 6 first-order differential equations, from which a super-Schwarzian function and 3 associated functions arise. The resulting supersymmetric action can be expressed in terms of 3 conformal weights and 1 new parameter derived from constraints on super-Schwarzians, providing a more comprehensive understanding of known actions. The conformal weights are found to be combinations of the principal grade and the grade of the highest-order superderivative in the associated K-matrices, offering a new perspective on known actions. The actions of 3-dimensional N=1 and N=2 supersymmetric extensions of the Schrödinger theory are derived and identified with previously known actions, revealing a new super-Schwarzian function and 3 associated functions in the former, while 3 conformal weights correspond to the 2 superderivative parameters in the latter. The super-Schwarzian function is found to be a linear combination of 2 superderivatives of 2 conformal weights and 1 new parameter.

The knowledge gained from rational dynamical systems and difference equations has significant implications in multiple disciplines, including systems biology, computational neuroscience, and population dynamics. Specifically, network science and the study of complex systems also benefit from these findings, as they rely on models that involve difference equations to describe the collective behavior of complex systems. In this work, we examine the stability properties of rational dynamical systems and provide fundamental theoretical insights into the stability of difference equation-based models. We derive new mathematical conditions that determine the stability of equilibria in rational dynamical systems and apply these results to a network model of population growth, showing how an individual's local model affects the overall network dynamics.

This paper examines an electrically charged, $(3+1)$-dimensional AdS black hole in a space dominated by a massive graviton, where the massive graviton follows a non-neutrino theory of general relativity combined with Einstein's general relativity and Maxwell's linear electrodynamics. The resulting equations are complex, so we use a known analytical solution as a basis and solve the system numerically. We explore the properties of the resulting charged AdS black hole, including its phase structure, behavior at its boundaries, and thermodynamic characteristics. The evidence we gather indicates that this black hole meets the laws of the Holographic Maxwell's Equations and further supports the issue that four-dimensional AdS black holes may have a theory of General Relativity combined with nonlinear electrodynamics.

The existence of Sidon sets, defined by $S$, for a linear form $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ with integer coefficients where $f(x_1, \ldotn x_n)$ is zero for every $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ in $S$ has been extensively studied. It has been proven that if the coefficients have a maximum absolute value of $M$, then $n$ must be at least $M + 1$. We show that if the coefficients are distinct and $M$ is less than $(2 + \sqrt{2})n - \sqrt{n}$, then it is possible to find an infinite $S$ which satisfies these conditions. This resolves a long-standing open problem set by a conjecture of Erd\H{o}s in 1963.

A connection between the geometric phase induced by an adiabatic process and the magnetic properties of materials near a critical point is established through the relationship between the magnetic susceptibility and the geometric phase. This link enables the susceptibility to be calculated from the geometric phase, and vice versa. This method is applied to three distinct models of systems undergoing quantum phase transitions, including the anisotropic XY model, the doped quantum Ising model, and the Kitaev model. The calculated results for susceptibility are found to be consistent with the outcomes from solving the differential equation describing the adiabatic process, as well as those obtained from the Schrödinger equation. Moreover, the calculated susceptibility exhibits a consistent behavior with the existing knowledge regarding these three models.

This research examines the changes in magnetization of a ferromagnetic material as it reaches its critical temperature when cooling from various high temperatures in a uniform magnetic field. Our findings show that when the initial state is above the critical temperature, spin fluctuations significantly impact the system's behavior, resulting in the absence of self-organization and the inability to create domains. In contrast, when the initial state is below the critical temperature, the system undergoes spontaneous spin reorientation in the direction of the magnetic field. Our research also reveals that the duration of the spin reorientation process depends on the initial distance from the critical temperature and the magnitude of the magnetic field. Our theoretical model's predictions match numerical simulations for the three-dimensional XY-spin system in the isotropic Heisenberg model.

Recent studies have extensively examined the cause-and-effect relationship between localization and quasiperiodicity in one-dimensional quasicrystal systems. While research has primarily focused on bound states, this paper explores the dynamical localization of resonant states under the influence of quasiperiodicity. Using the tight-binding model, we investigate the time-evolved density-of-states for various models of quasiperiodicity. Notably, our results reveal that the transition to localization is more closely tied to quasiperiodicity than previously thought, with implications extending to other systems.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages are typically trained using hand-labeled data collected from interactions between machines. However, this approach has a major limitation: it relies on manual data collection without the benefit of human guidance. As a result, there's a significant challenge in obtaining a substantial dataset. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel unsupervised technique for developing natively multilingual dialogue systems. This new approach enables a single high-quality dialogue system to be developed with a single model, utilizing a single set of well-structured, high-quality machine-generated data. Furthermore, we have created a benchmark dataset consisting of dialogue systems in four languages - English, German, Spanish, and Hindi - to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach. The experimental results demonstrate that our method produces high-quality systems, with the best system's performance being comparable to that of the best existing systems.

RNA-seq time series can be used to analyze differential expression and splicing through a coupled analysis of RNA-seq data and biological time points. A new method called DEADEE has been developed to handle this type of data by employing a hierarchical mixed effect model that models the relationships between time points. This approach accounts for time-varying gene effects, non-constant variation over time, and varying amounts of zero readings across time points through Poisson distribution. A new algorithm has been developed to compute the maximum likelihood estimates, and a simulation study has been conducted to demonstrate its efficiency. Additionally, two methods have been proposed to compute the posterior distributions of model parameters, and a case study has been performed using two models to investigate gene expression in Drosophila melanogaster.

To enhance data protection, organizations are implementing technical measures that engineers design, often without thorough discussion of their implications with legal experts. This lack of cooperation can lead to measures that fail to effectively protect sensitive data or impose unnecessary engineering costs. A proposed solution is to develop a tool that assists engineers in deciding which data protection measures to choose, taking into account the relevant data privacy laws. The new decision support tool, PPRDF, is a probabilistic model that combines data protection techniques and legal factors. PPRDF generates a chart ranking the most effective data protection methods, thus reducing the time and expense of engineering and legal teams finding acceptable solutions.

We develop a method to calculate the azimuthal fourth and fifth correlations
within the Color Glass Condensate framework for systems with intricate patterns.
This method expands upon previous research using the Martin-Sen model and
accounts for both initial and final geometry effects as well as fluctuations
in color and color coherence. Calculations reveal a theoretical basis for
azimuthal correlations observed in small system collisions, while also
providing insights into the physics behind correlations in multiple interactions
between particles and the effects of final state collisions.

The production of certain light nuclei, specifically a specific type of particle called the Z(+1) particle, has been studied using a specific computer model called the AMPT model. This computer model is based on actual data from a type of experiment called the RHIC by the PHENIX experiment. The research shows that the amount of these nuclei produced is heavily influenced by how they are formed. This influence also affects how these nuclei are distributed in relation to their energy. The research provides new information about how these nuclei are formed and what they look like. Additionally, it explores the potential reasons for differences between the research and actual experimental findings.

The discovery of multiple rocky exoplanets with planets 'b' and 'c' around K2-138 has sparked a new area of research, allowing us to explore the effects of orbital eccentricity on atmospheric loss and composition. We have simulated how different levels of atmospheric loss influence the chemical cycles in exoplanets with planets 'b' and 'c' over their 2.5 Gyr lifespan. Our results show that the unique orbital characteristics of K2-138b and 'c' lead to distinct differences in atmospheric loss rates, resulting in diverse atmospheric compositions. We found that the planets with higher eccentricities tend to have more water-rich atmospheres due to reduced photo-evaporation and efficient gas and silicate formation. In contrast, planets with lower eccentricities tend to have more N2-rich and less water-rich atmospheres. Our study highlights the importance of considering orbital eccentricity when characterizing the atmospheres of exoplanets.

This study examines the dispersal of the characters of circulant graphs with a maximum jump length of three, and determines their complete spectrum of dispersibility. The findings reveal that no new characters emerge in this class of graphs. Specifically, we identify the precise conditions under which new characters appear in regular circulant graphs, and establish a unique set of regular circulant graphs for each new character. Moreover, we develop a universal construction for all characters of regular circulant graphs with a prime power order, and this construction holds across all jump lengths. Furthermore, we categorize the new characters of regular circulant graphs with a prime order, and this classification is also applicable to the power of a prime. The research then extends to the analysis of the new characters of non-regular circulant graphs with a prime power order, and identifies the specific conditions under which these characters arise. The findings reveal that non-regular circulant graphs with a prime power order produce a complete set of new characters.

The Nested Neumann algorithm has been optimized for solving systems of nonlinear equations under pre-conditioning, and a key improvement has been made to improve its performance by incorporating the concept of inception depth. This modification is rooted in the observation that the convergence rate of the NN algorithm is directly influenced by the inception depth of the underlying network. By developing a novel method to dynamically determine the inception depth, the proposed framework enhances the applicability of the NN algorithm to a broader range of network sizes, thereby increasing its convergence rate. This advancement is particularly beneficial for addressing large-scale systems of nonlinear equations arising from the discretization of Maxwell's equations in electromagnetic nanocavity problems.

We've analyzed the influence of the cosmic friction term in the mode equation on curvature perturbations during single-field inflation. This analysis involved incorporating modifications to the gravitational sector, which could arise from certain dark matter theories, into the model. We considered a specific coupling to operators of dimension five and six, and calculated the corresponding boost effect on the power spectrum. We found that the cosmic friction term has a notable impact, causing the boost effect to be more pronounced than in the conventional Bessel function solution. This effect is significant, particularly in the long-wavelength regime, where the inflationary period or the radiation era can be reached. We compared our results to recent observations of the CMB anisotropy, and found that the dimension-five coupling, when it exists, can provide a suitable explanation for the observed phenomena, while also being compatible with the CMB measurements.

This study examines the effectiveness of offering limited flight prices, a practice known as revenue management, in scenarios where individual passengers may book seats for travel.  The model is developed under two conditions - one where the airline has complete control, and another where it doesn't, leading to an exploration of risk aversion among passengers in their decision-making process.  By analyzing both the extreme scenarios, the research aims to identify the optimal strategy for airlines.  The model's behavior in different contexts is thoroughly discussed, followed by an analysis of the impact of offering discounted fares on inducing demand and minimizing the loss of sales.  The underlying assumption is that, by offering restricted fares, the airline can create a greater supply of available seats without compromising its revenue per seat, thus increasing demand and reducing the negative consequences of underutilized capacity.  The model's validity is also evaluated through a simulation experiment where the research tests the effectiveness of offering limited flight prices, the optimal number of available seats to offer, and the potential loss of revenue from doing so.  The simulation results provide insights into the practical applications of the model's key findings, including the observation that offering limited flight prices can indeed lead to increased demand and revenue, albeit with a potential risk of loss.  The model's effectiveness is further supported by a case study of a major airline, demonstrating its potential to generate additional revenue while minimizing the negative consequences of underutilized capacity.  The study's findings also highlight the importance of offering limited flight prices to manage

The analysis of casebase studies, which only consider individuals with a specific event of interest, is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of treatments. A new package called casebase has been developed to simplify this type of analysis, providing an intuitive framework based on the casebase hazard process. This package builds upon the existing coxme and survival packages to offer enhanced statistical capabilities, including model diagnostics and goodness-of-fit tests. Notably, casebase includes several improvements over previous solutions, including improved asymptotic approximation and the incorporation of random effects. This package also allows for the estimation of point and interval estimates, as well as the calculation of power and sample size for statistical tests. Comprehensive examples demonstrate the package's capabilities and illustrate its potential applications in this area of research.

A new semi-numerical approach is developed to tackle the interactions of non-perturbative particles and colliders efficiently. By combining semi-classical and numerical techniques, this method achieves accuracy levels equivalent to five orders of magnitude better than conventional methods. As a result, it can handle complex, large-scale systems involving millions of particles without significant computational overhead. Notably, this approach has been successfully applied to simulate the behavior of superheated dielectrics in high-energy physics experiments.

Modern object storage systems are becoming increasingly preferred over traditional file systems due to their ability to scale better than legacy POSIX systems. In fact, Google's Filesystem specifically designed for Hadoop uses a global, distributed object model that supports efficient append operations, ensuring high scalability and consistency. However, the file system must also provide low latency and support concurrent reads and writes while maintaining strong file integrity. To achieve this, the file system must ensure that files are accurately and completely available even in the face of failures. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach that leverages distributed transactional logging to efficiently validate file operations, while also employing techniques to optimize transactional state such as caching and in-memory storage. To further improve performance, we utilize a hierarchical transactional log that is stored on a distributed file system, while also incorporating techniques to minimize the overhead of transactional logging. Our evaluation of the file system on a cluster of 576 nodes demonstrates its ability to provide high scalability and file availability while also significantly improving performance.

As electric vehicles (EVs) gain more popularity, their use of charging points is increasing, and managing these charging points is essential for both parking operators and EV users. A real-time pricing system called Fast-Charging Parking Spot Allocation (FP-2) addresses this issue by developing an advanced auction method that allocates limited charging resources to parking facilities while considering the users' preferences. This auction method, based on the Proportional, Incremental, and Multi-unit Auction model, optimizes charging point usage and user satisfaction. We evaluated FP-2 through simulations, comparing it to a first-come, first-served and a user-preference-based auction method. The results show that FP-2 outperforms the other methods in achieving proportional charging usage, reduces charging point utilization discrepancies, and enhances user satisfaction in terms of charging capacity and waiting time.

Our research centers on a specific class of codes known as Hermitian linear codes with decimal decoding, a subset of the recently introduced Hermitian linear codes. We develop general methods for generating new types of these codes using existing ones and propose a specific subclass derived from the first system of self-orthogonal codes. We further establish a connection between the new codes and finite field twisted Ramanujan graphs, and present some explicit examples.

In a recent study, the methods for calculating the $n^{th}$ order scattering cross-section of black-hole scattering in Einstein gravity combined with scalar interactions have been developed to $n^{(4)}$ accuracy. By applying a recursive technique to partial amplitudes, the process requires specific integrals up to $4n$, specifically up to $4n^{(4)}$. The research has determined these integrals and demonstrated their applicability to other general relativity scenarios, encompassing interactions with gravitons, photons, and fermions, thereby enabling the determination of high-order black-hole scattering cross-sections.

The rapid expansion of solar and wind power in the US will be crucial in meeting the nation's clean energy objectives, but the increasing competition for land use may intensify the risk of these sites' development, thereby affecting the affordability of deep energy transitions in some areas. To gauge the level of land use risk associated with solar and wind sites' locations, this research employs a novel metric that integrates data from various sources, including Zillow real estate records, to estimate the likelihood that a site's use will change. Our analysis of the potential land use risk for over 18,000 megawatts of solar capacity and 5,000 megawatts of wind sites across 15 states indicates that the use of both types of energy systems could impact the use of nearly 1.4 million homes, with significant effects on affordable and low-income households. Our results show that, compared to energy prices in other parts of the country, changes in land use risk may add significant costs to the affordability of electricity from renewable sources in some areas, with a potential increase of 4.5 to 7.4 US dollars per megawatt hour in certain regions.

Cluster-randomized trials are often used to assess the impact of a treatment on average outcomes within clusters, yet they fail to yield an estimable direct effect of the treatment on individual responses. This study investigates the indirect effects of the treatment on cluster-level averages through statistical modeling, focusing on generalized linear mixed effects models with varying levels of clustering complexity. The study provides a comprehensive framework for estimating a treatment's indirect effect, taking into account the distinct patterns of clustering that may occur. The proposed approach is validated through simulations conducted on diverse cluster sizes and treatment effects, and is further applied to analyze the impact of a low-intensity home visiting program on kindergarten readiness in the United States. The study offers a framework for implementing these methods in practice, utilizing available software and computational details.

This chapter focuses on deriving precise closed-form expressions for the topological indices known as the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index and the multiplicative arithmetic Kirchhoff index. Closed-form formulas are obtained for specific topological structures, including trees with $n$ vertices, and specific arborescens with $n$ vertices and particular edge configurations involving the vertex of highest degree. The text also outlines a method for obtaining closed-form expressions based on general mathematical structures.

We examine contextual linear bandits where the model for contextual data includes a distribution that captures prior knowledge.  We propose a contextual generalization of the linear bandit model and analyze it under specific assumptions on the context distribution.  We find that the requirements for communication can be reduced in proportion to the distribution's knowledge about the reward function.  This leads to a reduced communication complexity in several common models, including Gaussian distributions and binary contexts.  We find that our model's efficiency in communication remains optimal in key cases, particularly when the context distribution has a low entropy.

The impact of class imbalance on predictive models is often seen as a limitation, but it can be reversed by using oversampling techniques to concentrate the minority class, thereby actually enhancing the majority class, which in turn improves model performance. This unusual approach, or "majority bias," has been found to be effective in this reversal, and we explore its implications for machine learning model fairness. Our analysis shows that these models can be influenced by various factors, but the majority bias has a unique structure that sets it apart from other factors, and we provide a mathematical proof to support this. Additionally, we examine the connections between majority bias and other fairness-relevant concepts, such as counterfactual fairness and equalized odds, and our findings suggest that majority bias can be a key factor in achieving these other forms of fairness. Our results are based on a range of datasets and demonstrate that majority bias is a widespread and significant phenomenon.

The Heavy Flavor Ablation experiment at the Fermilab Pacheron fixed-target facility is designed to study the outcome of a single high-energy photon interacting with a beam particle, causing characteristic particle decays to occur. With data collection expected to begin in 2023, HFAB will generate a substantial dataset of approximately 10^11 meson decays, enabling various key measurements, including precise determinations of several key physical parameters in the Standard Model, such as the unitary-triangle angle gamma, charm mixing, and certain CP-violating interactions. The experiment will also explore unconventional areas of research, such as determining fundamental properties of the Standard Model particles and testing for signs of dark matter or alternative theories of nature.

A significant issue arises when research researchers struggle to independently verify and replicate each other's results. To tackle this problem, we propose an approach centered on the concept of universality, where the investigation of scientific concepts utilizes established frameworks and mathematical theories. By integrating mathematical insights into existing scientific research, we can enhance the process of reproducing and communicating research findings, ultimately contributing to their generalization and representativeness. To facilitate this process, we have developed a mathematical framework that enables researchers to track the progress of scientific concepts over time, thus providing a more nuanced understanding of each field. By applying this framework to a sample of 103 papers published in Physical Review Research, we have created visual representations that reveal the evolution of scientific concepts. Our results show that each paper can be effectively categorized using a mathematical framework, and our visual analysis provides valuable information on the connections and evolution of scientific concepts. By applying our framework to a large dataset, we have discovered that some papers are more influential than others in the field, and their authors may benefit from adapting their communication style to better convey their research findings to a broader audience.

A 'flying focus' Xerographer employs an X-ray laser to draw images with an externally movable focus, allowing for greater precision when creating detailed images in mid-air. By using a two-pulse technique, the focal point can be swiftly and flexibly relocated within a 5mm by 5mm 2D plane at a rate of 50Hz. This protocol's adaptability is illustrated through various laser writing, imaging, and sculpting applications, including forming intricate 3D structures with two materials at once, creating spatial separation of two materials in the air, and demonstrating real-time focus positioning through image capture. Additionally, the protocol showcases its resilience by successfully operating at lower fluence levels and utilizing a beam with 10% intensity loss.

The FIRA HuroCup league of humanoid robots has been actively participating in the International Robotics Olympics since 2004, completing the RoboCup 2017 5-aside challenge and looking forward to a new competition as a representative of humanoid robots. This paper outlines the development of a RoboCup 2017 5-aside game-playing robot, built on the ZHRUSHEK platform, and discusses the game strategy and navigation algorithms implemented for the robot. Simulations were conducted using Unity software to optimize the robot's movement, and a navigation algorithm based on the A* method was refined. This led to the development of a SLAM algorithm capable of mapping an unfamiliar environment and determining the RoboCup 2017 5-aside field layout accurately.

The cross-domain recommendation (CDR) issue is crucial in real-world applications. To address this, we've developed a new framework that enhances the performance of CDR by integrating it with metric learning. Our method, called DR&ML, utilizes a domain-specific embedding space transformed into a shared metric space, enabling the measurement of distance between users and items across different domains. By integrating a domain-agnostic head with domain-specific embeddings, we improve the predictive ability of the model. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DR&ML in addressing CDR issues, and our results show that incorporating metric learning can significantly boost the model's performance across three different scenarios.

We introduce an original automaton model that deviates from conventional approaches by allowing interaction between finite-state machines through a communication framework. In this framework, messages can be transmitted in real-time between machines, enabling interaction at the point of creation. The model's expressive power is demonstrated by mapping it to a pushdown word automaton with a non-collapsing stack. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that this model can replicate the computational capabilities of classical automata, while offering enhanced expressiveness in certain contexts. The model's versatility is highlighted by its ability to simulate various computational models, including multi-head automata, models with restricted look-aheads, and models operating on limited data.

A new model for heat transfer in a 2D complex plasma layer has been proposed, incorporating vibrational motion and its influence on plasma behavior through hydrostatic equilibrium. Calculations of the plasma's dielectric permittivity reveal that the vibrational model accounts for most of the experimentally observed inhibition of wave propagation in a CaTiSe$_4$ layer. Additionally, the model suggests a method for differentiating between surface tension originating from the liquid and electron liquid phases. The model's results are in agreement with the outcomes of a molecular dynamics simulation.

This paper introduces a novel, decidable method for evaluating the capabilities of counter machines with unordered data, and translates it into an equivalent Petri net model. The results reveal that this data structure can replicate the expressive possibilities of Petri nets with colouring, and our approach has implications for data flow graphs as well. Our research also explores the relationships between these machine models and other complex Petri net systems.

To improve image quality and reduce processing time for coronary angiography, we've developed a new method for creating high frame rate video from intermediate frames generated through motion estimation and interpolation. This approach uses a deep learning-based motion estimation technique, which is more efficient and accurate than traditional methods. Our results, based on a large clinical dataset, demonstrate that our deep learning-based method produces higher quality video with better signal-to-noise ratios than a standard interpolation method, particularly in areas with coronary arteries. Additionally, we found that motion errors are mainly caused by frame rate problems, rather than other factors.

The precise measurement of rare heavy-flavoured particle decays is crucial in understanding the fundamental nature of new heavy physics. The ultra-clean environment of the FCC-ee, achieved through its ultra-peripheral design, makes it an ideal location for this type of research. As a result, significant research efforts are being undertaken to investigate the properties of rare heavy-flavoured particle decays at FCC-ee. The following sections will outline the current state of this research, the challenges that still need to be addressed, and offer some thoughts on the future.

We provide a thorough examination of the $
u$TiME model, which enhances coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering, in the context of dark matter direct detection experiments. The analysis focuses on XENON1T's recent results, placing constraints on the $
u$TiME parameter space. Specifically, we find that these XENON1T results can limit the allowed dark matter masses below a few TeV, assuming minimal interactions between the dark matter and standard model. Furthermore, we consider how the $
u$TiME model can account for the recently discovered heavy dark matter particles in XENON100 and LUX experiments, assuming these events are indeed a result of dark matter-nucleus interactions.

This research examines how stars in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole are affected by gravitational disturbances caused by a companion star with a mass similar to that of the sun. The study focuses on the orbit of a second star in close proximity to the first star, under the influence of a perturbed orbit due to the companion's gravitational interaction. The theory of vector spherical harmonics is used to derive the gravitational disturbance, and the resulting equation is solved using the method of numerical Green's functions. The research then applies numerical simulations to study how the stars' orbits would behave in the presence of a protoplanetary disk surrounding the black hole.

This study investigates solutions to SDEs that have been perturbed by fractional Brownian motion, with drift and diffusion coefficients influenced by a solution to the Black-Scholes equation for European put options. We derive key bounds required to assess the option's value using such an approximation scheme. Ultimately, our findings show that when using such an approximation scheme, the choice of the Hurst parameter affects the scheme's accuracy, with H less than 0.5 resulting in overestimation but causing underestimation when H exceeds 0.5.

We demonstrate that a nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ can be described by a $\Sigma_1$ formula incorporating a set parameter if and only if it can be characterized by a $\Sigma_1$ formula without parameters from which a single element of the ideal can be deduced. Furthermore, we prove that if the ideal is countably complete, this equivalence holds only when it is characterized by a $\Pi_1$ formula. We also show that if the ideal is countably continuous, then it can be described by a $\Sigma_1$ formula with a set parameter if and only if it can be described by a $\Pi_1$ formula.

Multitask training is known to improve model generalization in supervised machine learning, but the optimal way to train these models remains unclear. Current methods often rely on limited or incomplete experiments to determine the best approach. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for multitask training based on the multitask training paradigm, involving a base task and multiple auxiliary tasks. Our approach allows for the systematic exploration of various training methods and provides a comprehensive experiment library that can be easily searched by users. Through our framework, we identified key findings, including the utility of multiple task experimentation in multitask training, the importance of selecting tasks with diverse characteristics, and the impact of task difficulty on model performance. We also discovered that task difficulty can be measured using a new metric that leverages the model's transferability and robustness.

The development of large-scale traffic sign datasets has significantly accelerated deep learning algorithms' ability to detect traffic signs. This paper presents MiSigns, a massive traffic sign dataset containing 540,000 signs located in 10,000 images obtained from globally distributed GPS coordinates. This dataset is designed to assess the efficacy of transfer learning across various scenarios, incorporating diverse traffic signs from numerous countries. To further enhance the evaluation process, 2,000 previously unseen images were manually annotated with GPS coordinates, while the remainder of the images in each country were automatically filtered based on geographical bounds. This results in a dataset comprising 239,000 images with unknown GPS coordinates and 301,000 images with annotated coordinates. To facilitate research, the dataset is made available under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License and can be accessed at http://misl.cs.cmu.edu/misigns/.

Recommending items with similar user preferences is a key objective of the recommendation task. Conventional approaches rely on labeling data with traditional supervised methods, but these methods often struggle with speed and scalability. To address this challenge, we introduce SelfCF, a novel framework that employs autoencoders to learn meaningful representations of user preferences in an unsupervised manner. By utilizing these representations, SelfCF is able to effectively recommend items with similar preferences. Moreover, to enhance recommendation accuracy, SelfCF incorporates a self-supervised contrastive learning module that leverages the abundant data to improve recommendation performance. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superior recommendation performance and remarkable training efficiency of SelfCF compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The enumeration of covers under specific ramification conditions of a given curve significantly differs from the straightforward application of the approach to general covers, as additional constraints are imposed on the ramification points. We will investigate ramified covers under specific conditions related to ramification indices and their residues, specifically looking at the implications of the Riemann-Hurwitz formula as a consequence of these additional constraints in the context of algebraic geometry.

We have investigated the electronic structure of a gapped Dirac semimetal, specifically the Cd3As2, using high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy. Our analysis reveals distinct characteristics in the spectrum that can be attributed to the Dirac dispersion, and we have accurately mapped its features using a two-dimensional approach. Our self-consistent band calculation aligns well with these features, consistent with prior theoretical predictions. Additionally, we have examined the influence of thermal effects on the material in this investigation. In a notable departure from prior studies, we have identified a distinct shift in the material's band structure at high temperatures, which we have attributed to a reduction in thermal energy causing a loss of three-dimensional characteristics, ultimately leading to a transition towards a two-dimensional Dirac dispersion.

We analyze a population dynamics model, represented by a two-dimensional differential system that incorporates delay periods and varying coefficients. The model's behavior, characterized by the system's trajectory patterns and the system's solution's boundedness, is examined as these periods and coefficients values increase. The proposed model, a modification of the classical Lotka-Volterra model, is used in population dynamics and has applications in other fields, such as biological systems with two species interacting periodically with their environment. The model's behavior is compared to its average counterpart under various mathematical and numerical conditions, with results indicating that the original system's behavior diverges from its average counterpart for large increase periods, and the period at which this divergence occurs depends on the system's initial conditions.

We have developed a method to calculate the binary black hole signal amplitude in principal component basis, which is suitable for binary black holes with arbitrary spin and mass ratios. This enables us to study the waveform's power spectrum and discoverability in space gravitational wave detectors. Our work has been applied to binary black hole coalescences with various spin and mass ratios, and we found that the signal detectability in principal component basis has a direct relationship with the binary black hole mass distribution. Our analysis also shows that the binary black hole merger rate distribution has a peak at approximately 10-20 solar masses with a certain spin and mass ratio, and we identified the binary black hole mass range that is most detectable by the space gravitational wave detectors. Our results indicate that the 3rd generation of gravitational wave detectors will be able to detect approximately 1.5-2 binary black hole coalescences with the binary black hole mass range of 100-200 solar masses with a certain spin and mass ratio, and we suggest that the binary black hole coalescences with the binary black hole mass range of 10-30 solar masses with a certain spin and mass ratio may be detectable by the space gravitational wave detectors with a certain signal-to-noise ratio. Our results also show that the binary black hole coalescences with the binary black hole mass range of 10-30 solar masses with a certain spin and mass ratio may be detectable by the space gravitational wave detectors with a certain

A binary system's motion can be analyzed through astrometry, but a new approach has been developed to detect compact binary systems using a specific statistical model. This method involves looking at the distribution of a system's motion over time, and by analyzing this curve, it's possible to detect binary systems with a mass ratio of less than 0.8 and distances under 100 parsecs. Additionally, this method was used to search for binary systems containing a black hole and found no such systems within a sample of 15,000 stars. However, this method can be affected by a star's shape and motion, and further studies are needed to refine its accuracy.

To effectively optimize complex optimization problems like the 0/1 knapsack problem, an efficient genetic algorithm needs well-designed crossover and selection techniques. In this study, various algorithms utilizing eight different crossover methods and five selection methods were developed to find the optimal solution for large-scale problems. Our findings indicate that specific combinations of crossover and selection methods can lead to the highest convergence rates, resulting in the best performance. Notably, the inclusion of a unique crossover-based selection method enabled the algorithm to outperform existing methods on well-known test cases.

This paper provides estimates for integrals of the form I_{T,Ω}(x) = ∫[0,T] Ω(θ^n) ^n dθ, with x ∈ ℝ^d and a polynomial boundary to 0 as θ → ∞ as part of an examination on the decay rates of oscillatory integrals.  It is observed that for oscillations with continuous phases, our approach yields improved estimates compared to those with polynomial phases.  It is also discovered that the most challenging case is when N = ∞.  Utilizing the previously established decay rates in an associated L^p → L^q Fourier extension inequality, we are able to derive L^p estimates for the oscillatory integral I_{T,Ω}(x) for x ∈ ℝ^d and 2 ≤ p ≤ q ≤ ∞.  Furthermore, for 2 ≤ p ≤ ∞, the estimates are seen to be optimal.  It is also demonstrated that the estimates are tight in the context of q = ∞.

The automatic detection of hate speech on Twitter has been the focus of various shared tasks in recent years. In 2020, the second iteration of the FAIRscope1 challenge focused on automatic hate speech identification, specifically on the Twitter platform. The challenge included a multi-class classification task, where participants had to classify hate tweets into predefined categories, encompassing distinct subtopics. A total of 72 teams from 18 countries took part in the competition. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the top-performing systems, highlighting the most effective approaches and highlighting areas for improvement. The results show that the shared task achieved high overall accuracy, with top models attaining maco F1 scores of 0.7996 and 0.7948 on two separate subtasks.

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations are known for their precision in replicating complex atomic and molecular properties. However, their computational expense is mainly attributed to the efficiency requirements of sampling the electronic configuration space. Our study demonstrates that the cost of QMC energy and force calculations is disproportionately increased when considering higher effective pseudopotential valence charges. To mitigate this, we propose an innovative approach that involves the addition of virtual orbitals, allowing the effective charge to be maintained while significantly reducing the computational cost. Our findings indicate that the addition of 6 virtual orbitals results in a minimal increase in error while achieving a substantial reduction in computational expense, yielding a $10^3$ times improvement in efficiency. Furthermore, we discovered that the addition of virtual orbitals also enables the accurate determination of ionization energies and electron affinities, a feat that is not possible with the standard approach.

As a company, Twitter has been working to curb the spread of misinformation, including the enforcement of a major 2020 US election-related rules policy update, aimed at curbing the spread of misinformation about voting and other forms of interference. In an effort to further understand how Twitter managed this, we investigated how it addressed claims of voter fraud on the platform in the days and weeks following the election.
