We explore cost-sensitive clustering methods and their implications for algorithm selection, suggesting cost-sensitive clustering can serve as a robust preprocessing step for addressing algorithm selection issues. We introduce a new benchmark dataset called adhoc1 and conduct a detailed analysis of cost-sensitive learning and clustering techniques. Our results indicate that using cost-sensitive learning for algorithm selection may not be effective and that cost-sensitive clustering offers a more suitable solution. We also propose using a cost-sensitive hierarchical clustering method that can help in identifying diverse algorithm configurations on adhoc1.

The 21cm background emission is a significant challenge for radio scientists due to its interference with the 21cm line signal, which holds cosmological information. To address this, a research team has developed an algorithm to simulate the 21cm background emission using the Planck Sky Model. The algorithm's components are explained in detail, and the team has created a data generator to produce realistic background emission maps. The generated maps were then applied to a 21cm signal analysis, helping to reduce systematics affecting the results. The algorithm's components are available for public use, as referenced in the citation link provided.

Research has been intensifying to discover novel two-dimensional semiconductors with high mobility and long-lived excitons to support high-performance optoelectronics and hydrogen storage capabilities. This study has identified Janus monolayers of Tm$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ as a type of stable p-type penta-hedron semiconductor. Notably, these monolayers possess a unique topological property and substantial spin-orbit coupling. The Janus Tm$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ monolayers exhibit semiconducting properties with a bandgap of approximately 0.55 eV and a room temperature Curie temperature above 2000 K. The optoelectronic characteristics of these monolayers are characterized by a high spin-orbit splitting of 0.43 eV and a high carrier mobility of 10,000 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The study also reveals that the Janus Tm$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ monolayers can be effectively integrated into a superlattice structure for potential applications in high-performance devices. The study further suggests that the Janus Tm$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ monolayers can be synthesized using a controlled method. The theoretical findings indicate that the Janus Tm$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ system has the potential to be used as a promising

Given two quasi-metric spaces, $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, and a positive definite function $f$ defined on $\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B}$, we can create two new positive definite functions on $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ respectively by applying a formula that involves function composition. This composition formula enables the construction of positive definite functions on the product space $\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B}$ in a systematic way. We have also obtained various results related to the composition of positive definite functions and the universal completion of quasi-metric spaces.

Positive monoids formed from geometric sequences have garnered substantial research attention due to their intricate structure and the difficulties in analyzing containment relationships between products of geometric sequences. We address this challenge by establishing a direct link between containment and divisibility within the context of products of geometric sequences. This connection enables us to derive separate characterizations of containment for finite and infinite products of geometric sequences. These findings not only enhance our comprehension of products of geometric sequences but also bridge the gap between containment and divisibility, making it possible to examine divisibility within the framework of products of geometric sequences.

Research has identified a link between certain diseases and environmental exposures.
However, studies that analyze this relationship may be biased due to the lack of
randomly assigned exposure controls. To address this limitation, researchers have
developed methods to create synthetic control groups using case description data.
In this study, we investigate the impact of case description data on the sensitivity
of exposure-effect relationship measurements in observational data. Specifically,
we propose a new method for measuring exposure effects and demonstrate that
it is more sensitive than traditional approaches when case description data is
available. Our method can be used to create counterfactual outcomes for cases in
the treatment group, provided that case description data is available for both
cases and control groups. Furthermore, we show that our method provides more
accurate estimates of exposure effects compared to existing methods. The proposed
method is flexible and applicable to a wide range of study designs.

Building upon the work of Keel, we build upon the relationship between the Chow groups of 0-cycles and Suslin homology in the context of normal projective schemes. This development allows for the expansion of existing findings on the relationship between Chow groups and Suslin homology in the context of smooth schemes (Blanc-Douaihy-Szamuely) to include the case of normal projective schemes.

A detailed analysis of elliptic and quadrupole flow fluctuations and correlations in mid-rapidity $p+$Pb collisions at a center of mass energy of 5.02 TeV is conducted using 3 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the ALICE detector. The study involves measuring the difference in flow coefficients and correlations between particles in various multiplicity bins and at different $\eta$-bins, revealing a complex relationship between the flow coefficients and particle multiplicity that cannot be fully explained by identified particle hadron and hadron momentum. The study also shows that the fluctuations in flow coefficients are consistent with those in second-order anisotropic flow coefficients across all studied bins. Furthermore, the fluctuations in quadrupole flow in high multiplicity events are found to be similar to second-order anisotropic flow coefficients, demonstrating a complex interplay between the flow fluctuations and particle production at hadronization.

Our experiment involves measuring the entropy of spin 1/2 particles using a protocol that leverages the multiple uses of a single measurement, eliminating the need for repeatedly applying a unitary transformation to a reference system. This method is an improvement over previous approaches, such as temperature control, erasure via a beam splitter, and using a microwave resonator, in which the reference system is left in a higher energy state. In contrast, our protocol involves entangling the system to produce multiple distinct outcomes, resulting in a more reliable measurement and reduced error, particularly for high entropies. This enhanced accuracy enables the direct correlation to be seen between the number of outcomes and the system's entropy, offering a more intuitive understanding of the concept.

This article presents the Geometric Modulus Principle (GMP) and showcases its versatility in proving a range of mathematical theorems, often yielding elegant proofs that are both concise and straightforward. Leveraging these principles can also facilitate the development of novel approaches to analysis. A new perspective is offered on the Intermediate Value Theorem, based on the principles of GMP. Additionally, the concept of Convergence theorems is explored in the context of Taylor and Laurent series expansions. Furthermore, the GMP is utilized to provide an intuitive and straightforward proof for the Fundamental Theorem of Integration. Lastly, the principles of GMP are applied to derive an innovative and straightforward approach to the Riemann-Darboux Theorem for improper integrals.

The discrete Schr\"odinger equation with long-range interaction is studied to prevent the collapse of its solitons by analyzing the behavior of the system's energy and norm. This analysis involves deriving an asymptotic series, which is derived from the asymptotics of the system's energy functional, and using it to establish a first-order asymptotic limit that governs the solitons' interaction and precision of the asymptotic expansion.

This research introduces a novel MM algorithm to address non-convex optimization problems with two types of constraints. It then applies this concept to complex cell planning in MMFS, which involves minimizing a cost function subject to signomial constraints and various linear limitations. To further enhance the efficiency of the MM algorithm for this specific problem, we introduce two novel proximal maps. Furthermore, we develop innovative MM updates and convergence theorems tailored to the unique requirements of signomial functions. This approach enables the development of a superior MM algorithm compared to traditional value engineering methods used in the literature. Our numerical analysis indicates that this algorithm outperforms standard value engineering techniques, reducing computational complexity by three times. Additionally, we propose a novel MM algorithm for addressing non-linear equality constraints in the form of polynomial equations, which exhibits global convergence properties.

A notable characteristic of hyperk\"ahler manifolds is their immunity to the Kobayashi hyperbolicity property. Specifically, even if a hyperk\"ahler manifold exhibits hyperbolicity in one of its complex structures, it remains non-Kobayashi hyperbolic across all such structures. Moreover, by extending this concept, any holomorphic fiber bundle over a hyperk\"ahler manifold also fails to satisfy Kobayashi hyperbolicity. This outcome also applies to Lagrangian twisted complex structures on a product manifold consisting of a hyperk\"ahler manifold and a torus, provided that the twisted complex structure exhibits holomorphic symmetry.

We introduce a cutting-edge method to automatically generate avatars from depth and RGB images in real-time, even when the input depth data is noisy and incomplete. Our system is based on a neural network that incorporates a new depth prediction technique, known as the Conditional Attention Depth Map, which leverages the corresponding RGB image to produce a more accurate depth map. This innovative method enables us to create avatars from both RGB and depth data as well as solely from RGB images in real-time. Our system's ability to handle noisy and incomplete depth data is achieved by utilizing a novel loss function and data augmentation techniques. Our system can also utilize pre-rendered 3D human meshes, eliminating the need for in-the-wild training data. Our research is the first to address the challenges of noisy and incomplete depth data in avatar generation using a single RGB image. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our system in creating high-quality avatars from both real and synthetic depth data in various scenarios, even when the input depth data is noisy and incomplete.

Recent advancements in face de-occlusion have garnered significant interest due to their practical applications. The majority of current methods, however, are restricted to scenarios involving single occlusions. This limitation makes these methods less effective in scenarios with multiple occlusions such as those created by various facial masks. This paper presents a novel face de-occlusion method that utilizes 3D morphable models to create a detailed, occlusion-aware facial surface. The method then utilizes a spatially-guided image alignment technique to register the restored face surface with the face image, ultimately resulting in a restored face image. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments conducted on the CelebA, CelebA-HQ, and 3D-Face-In-The-Middle datasets, producing de-occluded results superior to existing methods.

We've developed a novel reinforcement learning framework driven by intrinsically motivated behavior, where agents generate their own engaging rewards and utilize random goal generation to foster exploration without relying on external incentives. Unlike traditional exploration strategies, this approach naturally ties goal discovery to the value of reward acquisition, enabling agents to learn through dynamic and self-created challenges. Our theory predicts that, under specific conditions, this framework will result in effective exploration and optimal knowledge acquisition. To verify our theory, we tested the framework in a simulated environment with a gridworld setting, where agents successfully achieved optimal performance in both the training and testing phases without requiring any external guidance.

In a standard policy iteration algorithm, the optimal value function is approximated by iteratively replacing outdated values with a weighted average of current and neighboring values.  When considering an average of all current values, the optimality gap in a localized policy iteration algorithm decreases at a rate proportional to $1/k^{3/2}$, where $k$ is the number of iterations.  We investigate the impact of localized policy iteration, where each agent only considers a limited set of its neighbors.  We find that when the neighborhood size is $2k$, the optimization gap decreases at a rate proportional to $1/k^{3/2}$, the same rate as when all agents average values.  We also find that when the neighborhood size is $2k-1$, the optimisation gap decreases at a rate proportional to $1/k^2$, a slower rate compared to the case of considering all agents.  We also find that when the neighborhood size is $2k$, the optimisation gap decreases at a rate proportional to $1/k^{5/4}$, an even slower rate compared to the case of considering all agents.  We also investigate the impact of localized policy iteration, the average rate at which the agents reach the optimal value function.  We find that when the neighborhood size is $2k$, the average rate at which the agents reach the optimal value function decreases at a rate proportional to $1/k^{1/4}$, a faster rate compared to the case

The collaboration of NA49 and NA50 presented findings on the creation and dispersal of charged particles resulting from Pb--Pb collisions at 8.7 and 13 GeV per nucleon pair. Data on the distribution of charged particles was analyzed in relation to the interaction model using the Glauber model and the Monte Carlo method to establish the density of sources producing charged particles within the rapidity range. Comparisons with the NA49 and NA50 multiplicities, and the distribution of charged particles across rapidity revealed that calculations assuming no color-singlet interaction overestimated the data for events involving no charged particles, while underestimating the data for events with multiple charged particles.

Penta-silicene, a promising two-dimensional material, has garnered significant attention for its potential in next-generation electronics and optoelectronics. Unlike conventional materials, penta-silicene's energy bands exhibit non-parabolic characteristics under the influence of the energy-momentum plane's characteristics. This study investigates the third-order nonlinear optical properties of penta-silicene, taking into account its unique band structure and dipole selection rules. Under a linearly polarized optical field, a comprehensive nonlinear optical response is observed, comprising three distinct components, namely third-order linear susceptibility $\chi^{(3)}$, Kerr nonlinear refractive index $n_2$, and the Kerr nonlinear absorption coefficient $\beta$. The study examines the influence of the monolayer's energy bandgap, optical field strength, and the number of layers on these properties. Notably, the presence of a zero-energy gap in monolayer penta-silicene, as well as in its multilayer counterparts, leads to exceptionally large values of $\beta$, exceeding $10^{-21}$ m^2/W at a low optical field strength. This phenomenon is attributed to the significant impact of the Kerr nonlinear absorption coefficient $\beta$ in this regime. This study's findings provide valuable insights into the third-order nonlinear optical properties of penta-silicene and suggest its potential as a promising material for applications such as optical devices, sensors, and optical information processing systems.

In this research, we investigate the fractional Caldeira-Leggett (fCL) unification approach to describe the decomposition properties of heavy quarkonium, specifically focusing on its effects from the ground to excited states. The fractional parameter was then used to analyze the thermal decomposition of heavy quarkonia, revealing that the fCL method can effectively model the transition of quarkonium states at finite temperatures. The fCL method was also used to examine how medium effects alter the spatial size of quarkonia, with results indicating that the size of these states increases with increasing temperature, and this phenomenon intensifies as the heavy quark mass decreases. The fCL method has been shown to be an efficient means of studying the thermal characteristics of heavy quarkonia, and can potentially aid in the description of heavy meson interactions in medium.

The collision of the Earth with a dark matter subhalo could potentially leave behind residual effects in the Earth's geological composition. By analyzing the Earth's crust through radioactive dating of rocks and a detailed numerical model of the Earth, we identify regions where dark matter might have left indelible marks, leaving behind a trail of rocks altered by the encounter. This encounter could be re-created by a massive influx of dark matter particles, observed in the Earth's crust as a brief, intense spike in the neutrino flux, detectable by the next-generation of high-precision detectors. This dark matter model, characterized by a mass within a specific range and a relatively high interaction strength, is more consistent with the Earth's crust anomaly than models with higher or lower interaction strengths or masses outside this range.

This research examines the use of an uncertain reasoning approach in optimizing coordinated patrolling, where agents factor in their own uncertainty when making decisions. Our methodology is based on fuzzy logic, incorporating historical data and reliability factors to accurately reflect real-world conditions. We validate the effectiveness of our method through simulations of dynamic high-rise building patrolling, comparing it to both a basic probabilistic method and an optimal solution.

A groundbreaking neural network-based approach has been developed to address the issue of robot path planning and tracking in environments that feature both movable and stationary obstacles. This new method, known as the 'R^4' algorithm, successfully integrates path planning and tracking in real-time, while also allowing the robot to adapt and change course in response to its surroundings. This approach was tested using a mobile robot navigating through various complex simulated scenarios and achieved outstanding results, demonstrating a significant increase of 8.9% in navigation success rates and 23.5% improvement in trajectory quality over existing methods, while also reducing the number of planning points by 2.5 fold.

The phase diagram of a collection of dipoles arranged in a body-centered cubic lattice is analyzed. The phase diagram is divided into several regions, including a ferromagnetic state where dipoles align with their lattice neighbors, a ferromagnetic state with a two-fold symmetry where dipoles align in pairs, and a disordered state where no magnetic order exists. The phase diagram is also compared to a similar arrangement of dipoles in an atomic lattice. The comparison reveals that the phase diagram of the FCC lattice shares some similarities with that of the atomic lattice but has distinct features that are unique to systems of dipoles. The results are applicable to various physical systems, including magnetic materials with dipole interactions, spinor Bose-Einstein condensates, and optical systems that use dipolar interactions.

This study focuses on identifying a homogeneous inclusion with arbitrary conductivity using only exterior boundary measurements.  Our approach involves the transformation of the original partial differential problem into an algebraic problem through a Carleman weight that becomes exponentially large. This enables the solution of a strictly elliptic equation with exceptionally precise resolution. A key aspect of our method is establishing a novel observability result essential for obtaining a suitable Carleman weight. This result, independent of the inclusion's conductivity, is a primary contribution of this paper.

The study of magnetic field stability in stars is a key area of research due to its influence on the stellar structure and dynamics. This research investigates the stability of magnetic fields composed of a toroidal component, a poloidal component, and their mutual interaction. We demonstrate that these components are mutually stabilizing and suggest that this property plays a significant role in the formation of regular magnetic states in stars. This stability arises from the principle that parallel changes in the toroidal and poloidal components cannot occur independently of one another. This property is consistent with the observed patterns in the magnetic fields of stars and also explains the existence of stable, torque-free states in these stars. This research has significant implications for our understanding of regular magnetic states and their role in the formation of stable, torque-free magnetic fields in stars.

In a topological context, we investigate the behavior of the n-th order Kuramoto model, specifically focusing on how the network's ordered pairs of elements interact. Our work highlights key differences between the traditional complex network approach and a more refined method involving simplicial topology. Results indicate that this approach yields a more accurate description of the dynamics within the complex network, specifically regarding the emergence of synchronized states. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which these synchronized states can occur quickly, even faster than in the basic second-order Kuramoto model.

This study examines the optimization of the Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) operation on various computing platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, and CPUs+GPUs, by implementing different algorithms and memory layouts. In order to optimize SpMV on a specific system, one must consider a set of non-intuitive parameters, including the number of matrix entries, the number of matrix rows, the performance capabilities of the computing platform, and the memory characteristics of the platform. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of the optimal algorithm-memorization configuration for SpMV on a range of modern systems, and demonstrates how a simple analytical model can accurately predict performance by taking these parameters into account. This predictive model is validated through experiments on CPUs, GPUs, and CPUs+GPUs. This research is significant because it provides a simple, yet effective method for quickly determining the optimal SpMV algorithm for a given system, without the need for costly and time-consuming experiments. This approach can be particularly useful for users who are not experts in SpMV or algorithm selection and want to quickly find the best implementation for their specific use case.

Let $\mathscr{S}$ be a normal family of meromorphic functions in the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$ and $\{f_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}$ a family of meromorphic functions in $\mathbb{D}$. It has been proven that if the points of $\{f_{j}(z_0)\}_{j=1}^{n}$ are shared to a certain degree with the family $\mathscr{S}$ at a point $z_0\in \mathbb{D}$, then the family $\{f_{j}\}$ is also normal. This theorem has several significant implications, including a normal family theorem for sharing points with a normal family and a normal family theorem for sharing points with meromorphic solutions of higher order differential and difference equations.

To achieve human-robot collaboration on a large scale, especially in environments where the technology used is basic, it is essential to develop intention recognition systems that are robust and efficient. In this research, we evaluate the performance of various state-of-the-art methods for intention recognition from a single source of data, specifically audio, by using a dataset from a teleoperation system. Our goal is to determine a basic yet reliable model that can be applied to a range of tasks, such as navigating a robot in an unstructured environment, which can be achieved by comparing and combining existing results with a new simplified architecture. This comparison shows that the advanced methods can be simplified while still providing good recognition performance, leading to a more compact and efficient one-layer neural network model.

This paper establishes a comprehensive framework connecting homogeneous $n$-dimensional Monge-Amp\`ere systems to various first-order geometries through the lens of Lagrangian pairs. It establishes multiple key results, including novel characterizations, mappings that preserve complexity, and detailed mappings between these systems. Furthermore, the paper extends Hessian equations to a higher-dimensional context and reveals connections to the field of optimal transport. It also presents an alternative perspective on the $3$-dimensional Monge-Amp\`ere equation as a geometric problem in three-dimensional Euclidean space.

A two-dimensional computational model, integrating a two-fluid model coupled with a complex chemical reaction mechanism involving a detailed kinetic description of the hydrogen evolution process on metallic surfaces has been developed.  By comparing the electrolysis behavior of a gas diffusion electrode (GDE) and a plain surface, it has been observed that the natural convection influences the distribution of the bubbles in a significant manner.  A detailed analysis of the bubble dynamics in a GDE reveals that the convective motion plays a crucial role in the bubble distribution, while in the case of the plain surface, it has been observed that the natural convection has a substantial impact on the local mass flow rate of the bubbles towards the surface. The CMS experiment at the LHC has conducted comprehensive searches for long-lived particles produced during supersymmetry experiments.  A specialized trigger has been developed to detect charged particles generated by the decay of long-lived neutralinos, with a focus on their detection in proton-proton collisions occurring at a 13 TeV energy level.  The data collected by the CMS detector in 2017 and 2018, corresponding to 101 fb$^{-1}$ of luminosity, have been analyzed to identify signals deviating from the expected standard model outcomes.  A search for specific topological signatures, including charged particle tracks and delayed time-of-flight measurements, has revealed no significant signal enhancements beyond statistical fluctuations.  As a result, mass limits have been established for neutralinos decaying into charginos or sleptons, ranging from 460 to 1010 GeV, for particles with proper lifetimes between 0.1 $\mu$s and 10 years, depending on various experimental variables and supersymmetry models.  These findings significantly extend existing searches for long-lived particles into the previously unexplored range of longer lifetimes.

The temperature dependence of the specific heat in Dirac semimetals is investigated near the critical point, specifically how it relates to the critical exponent $\gamma$. It is found that the presence of spin-breaking terms in the Dirac fermion effective Hamiltonian significantly impacts the system's behavior, particularly when full rotational symmetry is present. However, when this symmetry is broken, the temperature-dependent correction to the system's behavior near the critical point leads to a specific form of the specific heat, $C_V(T) \sim T^3$, which is independent of $\gamma$. This effect becomes more pronounced at lower temperatures and is more noticeable in systems with larger spin-breaking terms, with potential implications for experiments measuring the specific heat of Dirac semimetals.

This paper proposes a novel method to transform sequential code into efficient concurrent code, leveraging Answer Set Programming techniques. By implementing a concurrent transformation framework, it demonstrates how to create concurrent code programs from a specific sequential coding language. An optimization approach based on a multi-objective strategy optimizes the generated concurrent programs, ensuring they execute quickly relative to their original sequential equivalents. To facilitate this, an explicit search algorithm is developed, accompanied by a formal proof of correctness. We represent the optimization problem as an ASP program and demonstrate its effectiveness through an empirical evaluation, showcasing substantial performance gains achieved by our approach.

A novel approach for testing the effects of gravity on small, isolated objects has been developed. This test involves observing and measuring the gravitational influence of a massive object on tiny test objects. The test requires a sophisticated setup consisting of (a) a highly stable environment for the test objects, (b) a system capable of detecting the test objects with great precision, and (c) a method to accurately measure the position of the test objects over an extended period. In an ideal setup, the test objects should be within 10 to the power of negative 17 meters of the test object, allowing for the measurement of a gravitational influence caused by masses as small as 10 to the power of 21 kilograms. The current limits on the graviton mass are 10 to the power of 23 hectoGeV, derived from the constraints of a detector capable of operating in a standard laboratory setting.

Observations from the ISO satellite's far infrared (FIR) camera provided a unique view into the chemical composition of a dark cloud in the Orion-Kent complex, located near Orion's molecular cloud.  The cloud's properties, specifically its low density and high gas-to-dust ratio, make it an ideal environment to study gas-phase reactions.  By analyzing FIR spectra, researchers were able to determine the abundance of C2H2, C3H6, c-C3H4, C4H6, and their respective isomers, as well as significant levels of CCH and CN, with the abundance of CCH being approximately 100 times greater than that of CN.  The abundance of C2H2 was found to be significantly lower than C3H6, with the abundance of C3H6 being nearly ten times greater than that of c-C3H4, and C4H6 being approximately three times more abundant than c-C3H4.  These results are consistent with theoretical predictions of relative abundances in a dark cloud environment, where gas-phase reactions are the dominant formation mechanism.

In our suggested model, a dark matter theory is established through a dark segment of a gauge group that extends beyond the standard model. This concept is based on the idea that the dark matter is composed of fermions with unusual properties that allow them to be part of a gauge group with asymmetric dark matter. This results in the creation of a Higgs-like field that causes the fermions to gain mass and develop a spin, leading to the breakdown of a gauge group symmetry. This, in turn, results in the generation of neutrino masses and the emergence of a dark Higgs field. This process also generates a baryon asymmetry and an explanation for the existence of the universe's small matter composition. This concept is testable through the study of dark matter's interactions with standard model particles.

Initial results from a search for the $t\bar{t}Z$ process in proton-proton collisions have been obtained using 2016 LHC data at 13 TeV. By analyzing 36 inverse femtobarns of data, the observed cross-section of the $t\bar{t}Z$ process was found to align with Standard Model predictions. This initial finding is supplemented with an updated measurement that leverages a combined fit of $t\bar{t}Z$ and $t\bar{t}W$ cross-sections, yielding a more precise estimate of the former's cross-section of 175 plusminus 25 nanobarns.

We provide a detailed classification of four-dimensional N=2 supergravity black hole solutions with STU models for four distinct black hole scenarios. These solutions correlate with semi-simple and mixed orbits under SU(4) in a concrete monopole decomposition framework. This outcome stems from our extensive analysis of N=2 supergravity with Abelian vectors, where we employed a systematic approach to integrate out the hypermultiplets, thereby revealing the underlying STU model structure. Our comprehensive study encompasses both asymptotically flat and asymptotically AdS spaces, and we identify potential avenues for extending our approach to other N=2 supergravity theories with vector multiplets.

In environments with partial observability, finding representations that allow agents to make informed decisions based on observations is crucial. A key concept, state representations, helps address this by enabling agents to consider the impact of past actions. Our work builds on existing knowledge by examining representations that also take into account expected outcomes. We find that incorporating this capability improves the accuracy of predictions in certain environments, but reveals a significant shortcoming: these representations struggle to consider multiple possible outcomes simultaneously. As a result, they fall short of providing an optimal balance between the influence of past actions and future predictions in guiding an agent's decisions. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework: reward-predictive state representations, which effectively combine the capabilities of their predecessors to provide a comprehensive framework for modeling various levels of uncertainty. Our framework's benefits are showcased through experiments in both simulated and real-world settings, where representations that incorporate both the influence of past actions and forecasting capabilities outperform those that focus on one aspect or lack this predictive capability.

Early warning systems are typically used to mitigate natural disaster risks, but can they be effectively applied to forecast less obvious social phenomena such as gentrification? This paper explores the application of early warning systems for gentrification in London, specifically targeting 33 London boroughs with a high likelihood of gentrification. It suggests that the knowledge gained from using these systems could be applied to other cities facing similar issues, and could ultimately help to address the problematical processes of displacement and housing unaffordability that gentrification causes.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on the transformation of skyrmion lattices in a 200 nm thick FeGe film under varying magnetic fields, temperatures, and propagation directions. Through a novel combination of magnetic field and heat, a stable skyrmion lattice transitions into a more stable ferromagnetic phase with minimal energy. Our results reveal that the transformation occurs through an unstable skyrmion phase, where the skyrmion structure breaks down and the system remains ferromagnetic. The research also explores the transformation's temperature dependence and resistance to reversing the magnetic field. Our findings support a two-stage process for the transformation: first, skyrmions merge into bubbles, and then bubbles collapse into a uniform ferromagnetic state, providing valuable insights into the creation and transformation of skyrmions.

This research classifies isometric composition composition operators within the realms of complex harmonic Bloch type spaces, ultimately leading to a comprehensive characterization of those operators in this specific context.

The growing demand for e-commerce has led to a sharp increase in urban delivery routes in recent years. This study focuses on how deploying range-extended vehicles within these routes impacts energy consumption and vehicle mileage. To achieve this, we utilize a robust optimization framework that takes into account various factors affecting routing decisions. By implementing a two-stage approach, we first solve a lower-level problem to generate optimal solutions within a restricted scenario. Next, we utilize these solutions to inform a solution to the original problem. This process is then iterated multiple times with varying vehicle mixes to achieve optimal outcomes. To evaluate the effectiveness of range-extended vehicles, we compare our model's findings to those obtained through a basic model without considering vehicle properties. This comparison reveals that incorporating range-extended vehicles can reduce energy costs by 7.6% and decrease vehicle mileage by 9.2% on average. Moreover, range-extended vehicles are shown to be more environmentally friendly than conventional vehicles in 70% of routes, with notable reductions in CO2 emissions. These findings demonstrate the potential of range-extended vehicles in reducing energy costs and minimizing environmental impact.

We compute the masses and leptonic decay constants of the light pseudoscalar mesons (mesons with heavy quarks set to zero) by applying the Bethe-Salpeter equation to the quark-antiquark system. Our results are obtained using a Regge motivated potential along with a specific quark-intermediate state approach. Our calculations agree well with the found experimental values. We also discuss the established connection between the BS wave functions and the properties of the mesons, allowing us to project our results to higher masses. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the specific introduced regularization on the integration over the BS time component.

This paper examines error bounds on the time derivative in numerical solutions obtained through the backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson methods. Building on earlier work, the findings are expanded to cover a broad range of problems, including those with non-smooth time-dependent components in partial differential equations. Specifically, the study demonstrates how previously established error bounds can be adapted to optimize the efficiency of the backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson methods, ultimately informing the development of low-stage Runge-Kutta methods that match the performance of these implicit methods.

Geo-spatial data analysis is a significant component of many business sectors, with researchers developing solutions to visualize large volumes of data from map services to enhance user efficiency. Despite advances, visualizing spatio-temporal data remains an intricate task. This study proposes a system for real-time system monitoring that leverages a geo-context aware visualization framework to facilitate end-users in visualizing and understanding the performance of autonomous driving models in a more intuitive manner. The system achieves this by incorporating the global driving context, visualizing the key features of the route and the model's prediction output, and providing a visual explanation of the prediction results. This monitoring framework has been successfully implemented and tested in an autonomous driving system.

A detailed model has been developed to account for the influence of photoionization on the behavior of GaN MESFETs, particularly focusing on the interaction between the gate, drain, and substrate. The model incorporates the impact of photoionization-induced charge modulation and the interaction between the gate and substrate, offering a comprehensive framework that can be applied across various operating modes. The model reveals that photoionization of the substrate has a significant influence on the device's drain current and associated noise characteristics under different operating conditions.

The model has been used to investigate the relationship between various noise parameters and the influence of photoionization on the device's performance, with a focus on the interplay between different types of noise and the system's response to various noise mechanisms. The study has shown that photoionization has a significant influence on the device's noise characteristics and can be used to develop a more accurate and comprehensive model of GaN MESFET noise behavior.

This paper introduces an innovative, data-driven approach to improve vehicle navigation system accuracy, particularly in scenarios with rapidly changing driving conditions. The proposed method incorporates a Gaussian Mixture Model to capture the evolution of vehicle trajectories over time, thereby enhancing location estimation reliability. Our simulation results confirm that this method yields more precise vehicle positioning, resulting in decreased overall positioning errors and a more stable positioning system in comparison with traditional Kalman Filter-based solutions.

A new method, called SG-PALM, has been developed to efficiently solve complex optimization problems. By using a unique 'zero-order' approach, SG-PALM can efficiently achieve local minima in various unconstrained and constrained optimization settings. The model uses an adaptive random process to locate the best solution by making adjustments to certain key variables. By doing so, SG-PALM can locate and maintain the optimal solution while avoiding getting stuck in inferior local minima. Furthermore, SG-PALM can leverage the power of graphics processing units to speed up the process. Theoretical evidence demonstrates the convergence of SG-PALM to the optimal solution for specific optimization problems. Experimental results show that SG-PALM outperforms other efficient methods for solving various optimization problems.

The Inertial Impedance (II) platform, which prevents objects from falling when there is an external force applied vertically, has been extensively studied as a research tool in active vibration isolation and control. We investigated the feasibility of using II to maintain a consistent and steady flow of objects falling from different heights using a basic Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller. We analyzed the performance of the II system when objects dropped from varying heights by measuring the II unit's II coefficient and comparing it to the II coefficient when there is no external force applied. We observed that the II system successfully achieved a consistent and steady object flow when there was no external force applied, and the performance of the II system, particularly its II coefficient, closely resembled its nominal value. We also found that the II coefficient did not change significantly despite repeated drops from different heights. We discuss the implications of these findings for potential applications in active control of flow systems and provide insights for future studies.

This paper presents a cache-based wireless network with delay constraints, focusing on network coding, user scheduling, and power distribution. It proposes a DRAKE algorithm, which combines a deep reinforcement learning approach with a kernel-based method. A user scheduling module, implemented using a convolutional layer, is enhanced by a Gaussian process to improve its performance. Similarly, the algorithm incorporates a two-stage power distribution scheme using a convolutional layer for training and a kernel adjustment method for improved results. Simulation results demonstrate that the DRAKE algorithm outperforms the baseline approach by up to 23% in terms of successful user ratio, 34% in terms of average delay, and 19% in terms of energy efficiency.

The PPT square conjecture has significant implications for complex matrices, 
operating within the context of a specific algebraic framework. It maintains 
a strong connection to a fundamental property in free probability, known as the 
R-circuit conjecture. Recent advancements in the study of matrix algebras 
have led to significant advancements in determining the stability of key 
conjectures under certain transformations. This study aims to provide new insights 
into the PPT square conjecture by applying a specific method to its 
mathematical structure. Specifically, we will investigate the relationship 
between the PPT square conjecture and other established conjectures by 
examining their stability within a specific algebraic structure. To do this, we 
will use a specific method to demonstrate the relationship between the PPT 
square conjecture and other established conjectures. It is found that the PPT 
square conjecture holds strong under a specific transformation, thus proving 
its' relationship with other established conjectures.

Given a group $G$ and its subgroup $C$ of inverse closed elements, we examine properties of the subgroup generated by elements of C that form a finite complete set of generators for $G$. We investigate the base mal-torsion nature of $G$, its 2-mal-torsion, and the subgroup $\Phi(G;C)$, which resembles the Frattini subgroup when $C$ is large enough or equals $G$. We investigate the base mal-torsion properties of $G$ when $C$ is the trivial subgroup or the whole group of $G$. We also analyze the conditions under which the $\omega(G)$ equals 1 and examine the consequences of the base mal-torsion properties on the nilpotency classes and solvability of $G$.

In ToA-based systems, placing anchors outside the target area's boundaries creates localization issues due to the center of the anchor placement causing significant errors. A novel approach, called the convex outer extension method, has been developed for robust anchor placement within and outside the target area. This method involves extending the area into a convex shape, placing anchors within it, and then using a weighted localization algorithm for effective anchor placement and accurate location detection. A performance comparison with existing methods is provided through simulation-based results, demonstrating improved accuracy and coverage in both inner and outer areas.

The development of x-ray diffraction under high-pressure conditions has enabled scientists to study the behavior of materials at incredibly high pressures, often reaching billions of atmospheres. Conversely, the optical spectroscopy technique is capable of exploring materials at pressures much lower than those attainable by an anvil. This research employs the principles of density functional theory to investigate the properties of materials at pressures between 0 and 100 GPa, focusing on the elements sodium through argon. Our analysis indicates that the shear modulus of certain elements increases with pressure, with a threshold around 100 GPa. By applying the Debye-Gr\"uneisen-Dynamical model, we determined the Gruneisen parameters for the elements and observed a notable distinction between the pressure derivatives of thermal enthalpy and entropy. This discrepancy is attributed to a change in the pressure dependence of thermal enthalpy to a value less than one at pressures exceeding 50 GPa.

Blind deblurring, a highly complex task, is further complicated by the lack of actual clear images to learn the blur kernel effectively. Most existing methods rely on optimizing both the deblurring process and the identification of clear images in conjunction, which hampers their performance significantly. To overcome this, our proposed method focuses on determining the most relevant patches from the blurry image that require deblurring separately, utilizing the blur kernel to achieve this, while the identified patches are then used to fine-tune the deblurring process. To address the issue of patch selection being too simplistic, our method introduces a reblurring module, which not only enhances the deblurring process but also refines the patch selection process. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method, making it a new benchmark for blind image deblurring.

A significant type of transient phenomenon, tidal disruption events (TDEs), occurs when a star's disruption by a supermassive black hole leads to a spectacular display of matter and radiation. TDEs are relatively rare, making up a small portion of transient observations, yet they can serve as valuable tools for understanding the behavior of supermassive black holes. TDEs are unique among these phenomena in that they can reveal information about the black holes that cause them. TDEs are detectable through a variety of signals including X-rays, optical, and non-thermal emissions, and a comprehensive analysis of these signs can help distinguish TDEs from other phenomena like active galactic nuclei and supernovae. Tidal disruption events can be predicted by the occurrence of a sudden increase in X-ray emission accompanied by a surge in optical light and a blue shift of the optical spectrum. TDEs can be further identified by the presence of a jet and a blue transient, and by a subsequent decrease in optical light as the debris from the star flows back towards the black hole due to the relativistic effects of the event.

The Ly$\alpha$ emitters are crucial for understanding galaxy development at early cosmic stages. Our research uses the Subaru telescope to observe the 822 square degrees of the Subaru-XMM $X$-MMXSS06 field, which overlaps with the XMM-Newton survey. By combining the Ly$\alpha$ emitters' redshift and galaxy properties, we can determine the evolution of the universe's matter density, the rate of star formation, and the properties of the intergalactic medium. Our observations were made using the Subaru telescope's V-band imaging and the cross-correlation with 2500 galaxy-identified clusters, which helped us identify 1116 Ly$\alpha$ emitters between 3.1 and 3.4. Our analysis revealed that the observed Ly$\alpha$ emitters' redshift distribution matches the predicted distribution from the dark matter map, which was created using the galaxy-identified clusters. Our findings also provide new constraints on the properties of the intergalactic medium and the rate of star formation at a redshift of 3.2.

We've conducted a comprehensive analysis of the reflectance spectra of 19 Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) in the cold population, based on observations from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) at the Dark Energy Experiment Site in the Chilean Atacama Desert's Cerro Pachon site. The TNOs in our sample were selected for their well-measured orbits, low albedo, and cold cluster membership. We compared these TNOs to 27 Ultra-Hyabellus Terrestrial (UTH) TNOs in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) database and 10 UTH TNOs in the Dark Energy Experiment database. We discovered that 9 of the 19 TNOs in our sample have albedo characteristics similar to those of UTH TNOs, suggesting a shared history among these TNOs.
